label: 0C
title: Collections & Loops: Tuples, Arrays, Vec
summary: Tuples, arrays and Vec; indexing and its panic; looping over lists; Option from get/pop/max; closures with iter/map/filter/sum/collect; sort and join; &[T] parameters as a view of a list.

quest.title: The Quartermaster's Lists
quest.story:
The quartermaster keeps everything in lists: crew names, barrel counts, the order of the night watches. Until now he kept them on scraps of sailcloth. Now he wants them in Rust, and you are the one who knows how.

Rust gives you three everyday ways to keep several values together. A **tuple** bundles a fixed handful of values of different types. An **array** holds a fixed number of values of one type. A **`Vec`** is a list that can grow and shrink. Add the loops and small *closures* that work on lists, and you can count, filter, sort and report on almost anything.

This is the last stop before Level 1. There you'll find out what really happens when a list or a `String` moves from one variable to another, and why you've been writing `&` in front of things.

concepts.title: Tuples: a few values together
concepts.body:
A tuple groups a fixed number of values, which may have different types:

```rust
let barrel: (&str, u32) = ("rum", 12);
println!("{} x{}", barrel.0, barrel.1);   // fields by position: .0, .1, …
let (name, count) = barrel;               // or unpack (destructure) it
```

Tuples are the easy way to **return two values** from a function:

```rust
fn min_max(a: i32, b: i32) -> (i32, i32) {
    if a < b { (a, b) } else { (b, a) }
}

let (low, high) = min_max(9, 4);   // low = 4, high = 9
```

`()` is the empty tuple, the "nothing" a function returns when it has no `-> Type`.

concepts.title: Arrays and Vec
concepts.body:
An **array** `[T; N]` has a fixed length that is part of its type:

```rust
let watches: [&str; 3] = ["first", "middle", "morning"];
let zeros = [0; 5];               // [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]
println!("{}", watches.len());    // 3
```

A **`Vec<T>`** is a growable list. You'll use it far more often:

```rust
let mut crew: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
crew.push(String::from("Anne"));
crew.push("Mary".to_string());
let barrels = vec![3, 5, 8];        // vec! builds a Vec from values
println!("{} {}", crew.len(), barrels.is_empty());   // 2 false
println!("{:?}", barrels);          // [3, 5, 8]: {:?} prints a whole list
let last = crew.pop();              // Some("Mary"): removes the last item
```

Like any variable, a `Vec` must be `let mut` before you can `push` or `pop`. Use `{:?}` (Debug) to print lists and tuples: plain `{}` doesn't work for them.

concepts.title: Indexing, get, and Option
Looping over a list
Lists as parameters: &[T]
Closures and iterator chains
concepts.body:
A **closure** is a small unnamed function written inline: `|x| x * 2` takes `x` and returns `x * 2`. Closures shine in **iterator chains**, which describe what to do with every item:

```rust
let barrels = vec![3, 5, 8, 12];

let total: u32 = barrels.iter().sum();                        // 28
let doubled: Vec<u32> = barrels.iter().map(|n| n * 2).collect();  // [6, 10, 16, 24]
let big: Vec<&u32> = barrels.iter().filter(|n| **n > 4).collect(); // [5, 8, 12]
let how_many = barrels.iter().filter(|n| **n > 4).count();     // 3
let words: Vec<&str> = "rum and gold".split_whitespace().collect();
```

- `iter()` walks the items, `map` transforms each one, and `filter` keeps the ones where the closure says `true`.
- `sum`, `count`, `max`, `min` and `collect` finish the chain. `collect` needs to know the type it builds, so write it on the `let` (`Vec<u32>`, `String`, …).
- Inside `filter`, the closure gets a look at a look, hence `**n`. Writing `.copied()` after `iter()` gives you plain numbers instead: `barrels.iter().copied().filter(|n| *n > 4)`.

A plain `for` loop is always fine too. Chains are just shorter once you're used to them.

concepts.title: Sorting and joining
concepts.body:
```rust
let mut crew = vec!["Mary", "anne", "Jack"];
crew.sort();                         // ["Jack", "Mary", "anne"]: byte order, capitals first
crew.sort_by_key(|n| n.to_lowercase());   // ["anne", "Jack", "Mary"]
crew.reverse();                      // ["Mary", "Jack", "anne"]
println!("{}", crew.join(", "));     // Mary, Jack, anne

let mut scores = vec![40, 7, 19];
scores.sort();                       // [7, 19, 40]
scores.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));     // [40, 19, 7]: descending
scores.dedup();                      // removes neighbouring duplicates
```

`sort` changes the list itself, so the list must be `let mut`. To keep the original, sort a copy: `let mut sorted = scores.clone();`. (Level 1 says when copies are needed. Here it is, deliberately.)

steps.note: A tuple lives right on the stack: its two fields side by side.
An array also lives on the stack. Its length (3) is fixed and part of its type.
vec! puts the items in a heap buffer. barrels holds a pointer, the length and the capacity.
push needs room for a 4th item. The buffer is full, so a bigger one (cap 6) is allocated and the items move over.
for n in &barrels: each n is a look at one item inside the buffer, not a copy of the list.
End of main: barrels frees its buffer. The tuple and the array just disappear with the stack frame.

challenges.title: The fourth barrel
challenges.story: Three barrels in the hold. The quartermaster asks for the fourth.
challenges.prompt: What happens when you compile and run this program?
hints: Positions start at 0. Which positions exist in a list of length 3?
Positions 0, 1 and 2. The compiler doesn't track how long a `Vec` is, so `barrels[3]` is only noticed at runtime.
It prints `total 16`, then panics: "index out of bounds: the len is 3 but the index is 3". Use `barrels.get(3)` when a position may be missing.

challenges.title: Doubled rations
challenges.story: Storm ahead. The cook doubles the rations, but only for the big barrels.
hints: Work through the chain one step at a time: first `map` (double everything), then `filter` (keep only the values over 8).
After `map`: `[4, 14, 8, 20]`. Which of those are greater than 8? And did any of this change `barrels`?
`[14, 20]`, sum `34`. `iter()` only looks at `barrels`, so it still has 4 items.

challenges.title: Fix the roster
challenges.story: The quartermaster's roster program won't compile. *Rustc* has two complaints.
challenges.prompt:
Make the program compile and print exactly:

```text
3 aboard: Anne, Jack, Mary
```

Rules:
- Keep building the list with `Vec::new()` and `push`.
- Keep the `println!` line as it is.
hints: Read *Rustc*'s first complaint: what must a variable be before `push` and `sort` can change it?
E0596: `crew` needs `let mut`. E0308: `len()` returns a `usize`, not a `u32`.
`let mut crew = Vec::new();` and `let count: usize = crew.len();` (or drop the `: u32` annotation).

require.message: Keep building the list with Vec::new() and push.

forbid.message: Keep building the list with Vec::new() and push, not vec!.

challenges.title: Barrel statistics
challenges.story: The quartermaster wants three numbers about the barrel counts, all from one function.
challenges.prompt:
Implement `fn stats(barrels: &[i32]) -> (i32, i32, i32)`. It returns a tuple **(smallest, largest, total)**.

- `stats(&[3, 9, 4])` → `(3, 9, 16)`
- An empty list returns `(0, 0, 0)`.
- Counts can be negative (barrels owed), e.g. `stats(&[-2, 5])` → `(-2, 5, 3)`.

Also implement `fn above(barrels: &[i32], limit: i32) -> Vec<i32>`: the counts strictly greater than `limit`, in their original order.

Hidden tests call both.
hints: Handle the empty list first with an early `return (0, 0, 0);`. After that, `barrels[0]` is safe as a starting value for both smallest and largest.

Loop `for n in barrels` and update three `mut` variables. Each `n` is a look (`&i32`), so write `*n` to get the number, or loop `for &n in barrels`. `a.min(b)` and `a.max(b)` help. For `above`, use a loop with `push`, or `iter().copied().filter(…).collect()`.
`let mut low = barrels[0]; let mut high = barrels[0]; let mut total = 0; for &n in barrels { low = low.min(n); high = high.max(n); total += n; } (low, high, total)`.

challenges.title: The watch bill
challenges.story: Every night the crew stands watch in pairs. The bosun writes the pairs down as tuples.
challenges.prompt:
A watch is a tuple `(&str, u32)`: a sailor's name and the hours they stood. Implement:

- `fn hours_for(watches: &[(&str, u32)], name: &str) -> u32`: the total hours of everyone called `name` (an exact match). 0 if they're not on the list.
- `fn busiest(watches: &[(&str, u32)]) -> Option<&str>`: the name of the **single watch** with the most hours. On a tie, the first one wins. `None` for an empty list.
- `fn roster(watches: &[(&str, u32)]) -> String`: every distinct name, sorted alphabetically, joined with `", "`. `""` for an empty list.

Hidden tests call all three.
hints: Loop over the list and unpack each tuple: `for (who, hours) in watches { … }`. Both are looks into the list, so use `*hours` for the number, or write the pattern as `for &(who, hours) in watches` to get plain copies. (The `'a` on `busiest` says the name you return comes from the list. Level 2 explains it, so leave it as it is.)

`busiest`: keep `let mut best_name: Option<&str> = None;` and `let mut best_hours = 0;`, and only replace them when `hours > best_hours`, or when nothing has been chosen yet. Strictly greater means the first one wins a tie. `roster`: collect the names in a `Vec<&str>`, skipping ones it already `contains(&who)`, then `sort()` and `join(", ")`.
`for &(who, hours) in watches { if best_name.is_none() || hours > best_hours { best_name = Some(who); best_hours = hours; } } best_name`.

challenges.title: Top of the leaderboard
challenges.story: The crew holds a knot-tying contest. The captain wants the podium, and a list of everyone who beat the average.
challenges.prompt:
Write two functions:

- `fn top_three(scores: &[u32]) -> Vec<u32>`: the three highest scores, highest first. Duplicates count separately (`[5, 9, 9, 1]` → `[9, 9, 5]`). With fewer than three scores, return all of them, sorted highest first. Don't change the caller's list.
- `fn above_average(scores: &[u32]) -> usize`: how many scores are **strictly** above the average. Compare exactly: `[1, 2]` has average 1.5, so one score (2) is above it. An empty list gives `0`.

Keep a `fn main()`; it can print something or stay empty. Hidden tests call both. After they pass, the tutor judges whether your solution is idiomatic.
challenges.starter:
// Write top_three(scores: &[u32]) -> Vec<u32> and above_average(scores: &[u32]) -> usize here.

fn main() {}
hints: `top_three`: you may not sort the caller's list, so make your own copy first: `let mut sorted = scores.to_vec();`. Then sort it highest first and keep the first three.

`sorted.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))` sorts in descending order (or `sort()` then `reverse()`). `sorted.truncate(3)` keeps at most three items. For the average, `total as f64 / len as f64` works. An integer-only trick: `s` is above the average exactly when `s * len > total`.
`scores.iter().filter(|&&s| s as f64 > avg).count()`. Or a `for` loop with a counter, which is just as good. Remember the empty list: return early before dividing by zero.
challenges.rubric: Idiomatic beginner collection handling: parameters are `&[u32]` slices and the caller's list is not modified (an owned copy via `to_vec()`/`clone()` is made only for sorting, which is fine and expected). `top_three` sorts descending (`sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a))`, `sort` + `reverse`, or `sort_unstable_by`) and then `truncate(3)`, `take(3).collect()` or similar. Manual index juggling that duplicates sort logic is weaker. `above_average` handles the empty list before dividing, and avoids integer division that rounds the average down (using f64 or the `s * n > total` trick). Overflow-safe summation (u64) is a plus but not required. Iterator chains or plain `for` loops with counters are equally acceptable; reward clarity. Deduct for `unwrap()` on values that can be empty, for indexing past the end, or for needless clones inside loops.

challenges.title: Boss: Muster on deck
challenges.story: All hands on deck! The quartermaster reads out the muster: names and ages, one sailor per line, some lines blotted by sea spray. The captain wants the summary before the anchor is up.
challenges.prompt:
The program reads **all of stdin**. Each line should be `name age`: a name with no spaces, whitespace, then an age that fits in `u32`. Lines are trimmed first, and empty lines are skipped. Any other non-empty line (wrong number of words, or an age that doesn't parse) counts as **blotted**.

Print exactly these lines:

1. `crew: N` (the number of valid sailors)
2. `blotted: B`
3. `oldest: NAME (AGE)`, the first sailor with the highest age, or `oldest: none` if there are no sailors
4. `average age: A`, the average with exactly one decimal (`{:.1}`), or `average age: none`
5. `roster: NAMES`, the names sorted alphabetically (byte order, as `sort()` does), joined with `", "`, or `roster: none`

For this input:

```text
Anne 31
Jack 42
Mary 29
Bo   42
smudge
Ned old

Zed 17
```

the output is exactly:

```text
crew: 5
blotted: 2
oldest: Jack (42)
average age: 32.2
roster: Anne, Bo, Jack, Mary, Zed
```

The hidden cases include empty input, a muster with only blotted lines, and padded lines. Use the **stdin** box next to Run to try your own input.
hints: First turn the text into data: a `Vec<(&str, u32)>` of sailors plus a `blotted` counter. Then compute the five lines from that `Vec`. A helper `fn parse_sailor(line: &str) -> Option<(&str, u32)>` keeps `main` short.

To parse a line: `let words: Vec<&str> = line.split_whitespace().collect();`. It's valid if `words.len() == 2` and `words[1].parse::<u32>()` is `Ok(age)`. Use `match` or `if let Ok(age) = …` on the parse.

Oldest: keep `Option<(&str, u32)>` and replace it only when the new age is **strictly** greater (the first one wins a tie). Average: `total as f64 / crew.len() as f64`, printed with `{:.1}`. Watch the empty crew: check `crew.is_empty()` before dividing.

Roster: `let mut names: Vec<&str> = crew.iter().map(|&(name, _)| name).collect(); names.sort(); names.join(", ")`. If the closure pattern feels odd, a `for` loop that pushes `name` works just as well.

cards.front: How do you read the fields of `let barrel = ("rum", 12);`, and how do you return two values from a function?
cards.back: By position, `barrel.0` and `barrel.1`, or by unpacking: `let (name, count) = barrel;`. Return a tuple: `fn min_max(…) -> (i32, i32) { (low, high) }`.

An array has a fixed length that is part of its type, e.g. `[i32; 3]`, and lives on the stack. A `Vec` can grow and shrink (`push`, `pop`), and its items live on the heap. `vec![1, 2, 3]` builds a `Vec`.

cards.front: What does `v[3]` do on a 3-item `Vec`, and what's the safe alternative?
cards.back: It **panics** at runtime: index out of bounds (positions are 0, 1, 2). `v.get(3)` returns `None` instead; it returns `Some(&item)` when the position exists.

cards.front: Which list methods return an `Option`, and three ways to handle one?
cards.back: `get`, `first`, `last`, `pop`, `iter().max()`, `iter().min()`, because the list may be empty or too short. Handle it with `match x { Some(v) => …, None => … }`, with `if let Some(v) = x { … }`, or with `x.unwrap_or(default)`.

`map(|x| …)` transforms each item, and `filter(|x| …)` keeps the items where the closure returns `true`. `sum`, `count` and `collect` finish the chain: add up, count, or build a new collection. `collect` needs the target type, e.g. `let v: Vec<u32> = …`.
A **closure**: a small unnamed function written inline. Parameters go between the bars, and the body follows. Used with `map`, `filter`, `sort_by` and more. `|a, b| b.cmp(a)` takes two parameters.

cards.front: Why does `let crew = Vec::new(); crew.push("Anne");` fail?
cards.back: E0596: `push` changes the list, and `crew` isn't `mut`. Write `let mut crew = Vec::new();`. Also note that `len()` returns a `usize`, not a `u32`.

cards.front: `for x in &v` vs `for x in v` vs `for x in v.iter_mut()`?
cards.back: `&v` looks at each item, and `v` stays usable. Plain `v` uses the list up, so it can't be used afterwards (Level 1 explains why). `iter_mut()` lets you change each item through `*x`.

cards.front: What parameter type should a function that only reads a list of `i32` take, and how do you call it?
cards.back: `&[i32]`, a slice (a view of a list). Call it with `f(&my_vec)` or `f(&my_array)`. It's the list counterpart of `&str` for text.

cards.front: Sort a `Vec` descending, keep the first three, and join text with commas?
cards.back: `v.sort_by(|a, b| b.cmp(a));` (or `sort()` then `reverse()`), then `v.truncate(3);`. For text lists, `names.join(", ")`. Sorting changes the list, so it must be `mut`. Sort a `to_vec()` copy to keep the original.
